Question: Can agents write, execute, and iterate code in isolated environments? Which runtimes are supported (Python, JS, SQL minimum)?
Response: Yes. A MAF agent executor — i.e. a GHCP SDK session invoked from a MAF agent node — can generate and execute code in sandboxed environments. Python is natively supported (GHCP SDK is Python-based). For sandboxed execution: Azure Container Apps or Azure Container Instances provide isolated runtime environments. The agent executor generates code (e.g. CV parsing logic, data transformation, analytics queries), executes it in the sandbox, evaluates results and iterates; a downstream MAF validator executor asserts schema and policy on the output before it propagates. SQL execution against data stores (Cosmos DB, Dataverse, Databricks SQL Warehouse, Snowflake) is supported via MCP tool calls — Databricks and Snowflake remain in place under Unity Catalog and Snowflake governance; Fabric IQ federates via OneLake shortcuts when ontology-level reasoning is required. JavaScript in sandboxed Node.js environments. All generated code execution is governed: GHCP SDK hooks log code generation events, Foundry Guardrails inspect code for safety inside the session, the MAF validator enforces structure on typed output, and the sandbox isolates production systems.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK (code generation), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 agent + validator executors, Azure Container Apps/Instances (sandbox), Python/JS/SQL runtimes
POC Demo: POC2: Show CV parsing code generated and executed in sandbox — a MAF agent executor (GHCP SDK session) writes a Python parser, runs it on test data, a validator executor asserts structure, and the pattern iterates.

Question: Can proven generative code solutions be reviewed, tested, versioned, and promoted into a managed function library with CI/CD; becoming deterministic tools callable by agents?
Response: Yes — this is the core crystallisation mechanism, and in our architecture it is structural: an agent executor node in the MAF workflow graph is replaced by a deterministic plain-function executor, with the agent executor preserved on a conditional-edge fallback for low-confidence cases. Pipeline: (1) Agent executor generates code solution (e.g. CV parsing logic); validator executor downstream asserts structure. (2) After N successful runs with rare human overrides, the solution is submitted for human review via the Control Plane. (3) Reviewed code is committed to Git and registered as a skill in Azure API Center at Design stage. (4) CI/CD runs unit tests, integration tests, evaluation against test data (APIOps approval gates). (5) Promoted: Design → Preview → Production. (6) The MAF workflow graph is updated to route happy-path traffic to the deterministic plain-function executor — faster, cheaper, more predictable. (7) The low-confidence branch still routes to the original agent executor as a fallback. Skills are Git-synced via GitHub Actions to API Center. GHCP SDK hooks ensure agent executors pick up promoted skills automatically.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (lifecycle), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph (agent → plain-function executor migration), Git, APIOps CI/CD pipeline, GHCP SDK hooks, SKILL.md
POC Demo: POC2: Demonstrate full crystallisation pipeline — CV parser promoted from generative to deterministic skill. Show approval gate in API Center and fallback on novel input.

Question: Can agents operate headless browsers or VMs to interact with web applications; integrated with enterprise IDAM (Okta/Entra ID)? Can generated automation scripts be reviewed, frozen, containerised?
Response: GHCP SDK supports computer use patterns — an agent executor (GHCP SDK session) inside a MAF agent node can drive a headless browser via Playwright or similar to interact with legacy web applications. For enterprise IDAM integration: the browser session authenticates via Okta/Entra ID using the Hosted Agent's identity, with Conditional Access policies applying. Generated automation scripts follow the crystallisation pipeline: (1) agent executor generates the script, (2) human reviews via Control Plane, (3) approved script is frozen, containerised, and registered as a deterministic plain-function executor in the MAF graph — with the agent executor preserved as a fallback. Primarily useful for legacy HR systems without APIs.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK computer use, Playwright, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph, Entra/Okta IDAM, crystallisation pipeline

Question: Describe the review gate for generated scripts: approval workflow, immutability post-approval, version control, audit trail, execution log retention.
Response: Script governance uses the same skill lifecycle pipeline. (1) Approval workflow: generated scripts submitted via the Control Plane for human review; API Center lifecycle gates approval Design → Preview → Production. (2) Immutability: once promoted to Production, the skill version is immutable; modification requires a new version through the full lifecycle. (3) Version control: skills and MAF workflow graph definitions are Git-committed; API Center maintains full version history. (4) Audit trail: every script execution is logged in OTEL — MAF workflow spans emitted natively, GHCP SDK session spans (inside agent executors) emitted via the SDK TracerProvider, with what inputs and outputs. GHCP SDK hooks log all tool calls including script executions. (5) Execution log retention: all logs flow to Azure Log Analytics with 7-12 year retention (immutability via Azure Storage export with immutability policies). Approval decisions logged with approver identity and timestamp.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center lifecycle, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph versioning, Git version control, OTEL execution logging (MAF + GHCP SDK), Azure Log Analytics
